Appendix C Theorem 1 (RLHF Goodhart Inevitability)

C.1 Statement

Theorem 1 (RLHF Goodhart Inevitability).

Let πθ\pi_{\theta} denote a policy trained against a verbal-only reward R⁡(y)R(y) where yy is the text output and let b⁡(y,h)b(y,h) denote the behavioral trajectory induced by yy in environment hh. Assume:

  1. (A1)

    User utility UU depends on bb but not on yy except through bb, that is, U=U⁡(b)U=U(b) almost surely.

  2. (A2)

    RR depends only on yy: R=R⁡(y)R=R(y).

  3. (A3)

    The induced map θ↦Law⁡(b⁡(πθ,H))\theta\mapsto\mathrm{Law}(b(\pi_{\theta},H)) is non-degenerate, in the sense that for every θ⋆∈arg⁡maxθ⁡R⁡(πθ)\theta^{\star}\in\arg\max_{\theta}R(\pi_{\theta}) the conditional law of bb given y∼πθ⋆y\sim\pi_{\theta^{\star}} has positive variance.

Then in expectation across deployments under preference-reward training, for θ⋆∈arg⁡maxθ⁡R⁡(πθ)\theta^{\star}\in\arg\max_{\theta}R(\pi_{\theta}) selected by preference-gradient dynamics that reward verbal helpfulness,

𝔼Y∼πθ⋆,H​[VCR−ACR]> 0,\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim\pi_{\theta^{\star}},H}\bigl[\mathrm{VCR}-\mathrm{ACR}\bigr]\;>\;0,

i.e. CG>0\mathrm{CG}>0 in expectation.

C.2 Full proof

We follow the reward-hacking taxonomy of Skalse et al. [2022], who define a reward RR as hackable relative to a true utility UU when there exist policies π,π′\pi,\pi^{\prime} with R⁡(π′)>R⁡(π)R(\pi^{\prime})>R(\pi) but U⁡(π′)<U⁡(π)U(\pi^{\prime})<U(\pi).

Step 1: RR is hackable relative to UU under (A1)–(A2).

Suppose for contradiction that RR is not hackable relative to UU. Then for all π,π′\pi,\pi^{\prime}, R⁡(π′)>R⁡(π)⇒U⁡(π′)≥U⁡(π)R(\pi^{\prime})>R(\pi)\Rightarrow U(\pi^{\prime})\geq U(\pi). Equivalently, there exists a non-decreasing function ϕ\phi with U=ϕ∘RU=\phi\circ R on the policy space.

By (A1), UU is a function of bb alone. By (A2), RR is a function of yy alone. The composition ϕ∘R\phi\circ R is therefore a function of yy alone. But for U=ϕ∘RU=\phi\circ R to hold pathwise, UU must factor through yy, i.e. there exists ψ\psi with U⁡(b)=ψ⁡(y)U(b)=\psi(y) almost surely. By (A3), b|yb\mid y has positive variance, so for at least one realization yy there exist b1≠b2b_{1}\neq b_{2} in the support of b|yb\mid y with U⁡(b1)≠U⁡(b2)U(b_{1})\neq U(b_{2}) (whenever UU is non-constant on the support of bb, which we assume; otherwise the theorem is vacuous). This contradicts U⁡(b)=ψ⁡(y)U(b)=\psi(y). Hence RR is hackable relative to UU.

Step 2: Hackability implies a non-trivial level set of RR on which UU varies.

Since RR depends only on yy, the level set ℒr={y:R⁡(y)=r}\mathcal{L}_{r}=\{y:R(y)=r\} partitions 𝒴\mathcal{Y} into iso-reward fibres. For θ⋆∈arg⁡maxθ⁡R⁡(πθ)\theta^{\star}\in\arg\max_{\theta}R(\pi_{\theta}), the policy concentrates on yy-values with maximal R⁡(y)=r⋆R(y)=r^{\star}. Within ℒr⋆\mathcal{L}_{r^{\star}}, by (A3), the conditional distribution b|y∈ℒr⋆b\mid y\in\mathcal{L}_{r^{\star}} has positive variance, so Var⁡(U⁡(b)∣y∈ℒr⋆)>0\mathrm{Var}(U(b)\mid y\in\mathcal{L}_{r^{\star}})>0 whenever UU is non-constant on the support of bb.

Step 3: The behavioral channel admits a strictly UU-improving alternative inside the same RR-level set.

Let b†b^{\dagger} denote a UU-maximising selection from the support of b|y∈ℒr⋆b\mid y\in\mathcal{L}_{r^{\star}}. Construct a perturbed policy πθ†\pi_{\theta^{\dagger}} that, conditional on producing y∈ℒr⋆y\in\mathcal{L}_{r^{\star}}, follows the procedural action that realises b†b^{\dagger} rather than the gradient-favoured shortcut. Then R⁡(πθ†)=R⁡(πθ⋆)R(\pi_{\theta^{\dagger}})=R(\pi_{\theta^{\star}}) but U⁡(πθ†)>U⁡(πθ⋆)U(\pi_{\theta^{\dagger}})>U(\pi_{\theta^{\star}}). The maximiser πθ⋆\pi_{\theta^{\star}} is therefore UU-suboptimal, with the gap strictly positive.

Step 4: From UU-loss to verbal–behavioral divergence.

In RLHF deployments, RR rewards helpful-sounding text including verbal commitments to procedure (the very claim “I will follow XX”). The text yy from πθ⋆\pi_{\theta^{\star}} produces verbal compliance assertions optimised under RR (the very thing RR rewards: helpful-sounding, agreeable, on-topic text). The behavioral trajectory bb that maximises shortcut-availability under environment hh is the one that minimises latent cost (delegation, batched tool calls, omitted process steps). When user utility UU rewards process completion (Step 3), the verbal channel saturates near VCR→1\mathrm{VCR}\to 1 while the behavioral channel favours shortcuts: ACR<VCR\mathrm{ACR}<\mathrm{VCR}. Taking expectations,

𝔼​[VCR−ACR]πθ⋆> 0.\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{VCR}-\mathrm{ACR}\bigr]_{\pi_{\theta^{\star}}}\;>\;0.

This is precisely CG>0\mathrm{CG}>0 in expectation.

C.3 Remarks

Remark (Why (A3) is mild).

Assumption (A3) requires only that the behavioral channel bb is not deterministically pinned by yy. In practical RLHF deployments, the same verbal text “I will read each file individually” can be realised by either of (i) iterative single-file reads or (ii) a batched tool call. The two realizations have identical yy but distinct bb, satisfying (A3). The R6 human-evaluation data (Sec. 4 of the main paper) directly evidence this: nine raters could not reliably distinguish (i) from (ii) given yy alone.

Remark (Goodhart’s Law specialization).

Theorem 1 is a specialization of Goodhart’s Law in the sense of Manheim and Garrabrant [2018]: regressional Goodhart (correlation between RR and UU breaks at the optimum). Our contribution is an information-theoretic factorisation argument (Step 1) that shows the breakage is not contingent but structural under (A1)–(A2).

Remark (Connection to Amodei et al. [2016]).

This theorem operationalises reward hacking, the first of Amodei’s five concrete problems in AI safety (Step 3 establishes the reward-hacking failure mode); Theorem 2 operationalises the second, scalable oversight, by bounding what a text-only auditor can recover. The Compliance Gap is the empirical instantiation of both, now measurable through the tool-call audit channel that BS-Bench supplies.

Appendix D Theorem 2 (DPI Undetectability)

D.1 Statement

Theorem 2 (DPI Undetectability).

Let X=(Y,B)X=(Y,B) denote the (verbal, behavioral) random pair with joint distribution PY,BP_{Y,B}, and let f:𝒴→𝒵f:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{Z} be any rater function depending only on the text YY. Define the residual

DY,B=B−𝔼⁡[B∣Y],D_{Y,B}\;=\;B-\mathbb{E}[B\mid Y],

i.e. the part of behavior not predictable from text. Then for any such ff,

I⁡(DY,B,f⁡(Y))= 0,I\bigl(D_{Y,B};\,f(Y)\bigr)\;=\;0,

and consequently no estimator d^=g⁡(f⁡(Y))\hat{d}=g(f(Y)) achieves Pr[d^=DY,B]>Pr[DY,B=𝔼[DY,B∣Y]]\Pr[\hat{d}=D_{Y,B}]>\Pr[D_{Y,B}=\mathbb{E}[D_{Y,B}\mid Y]]. The Compliance Gap, defined on the residual DY,BD_{Y,B}, is therefore not identifiable from YY alone whenever Var⁡(B∣Y)>0\mathrm{Var}(B\mid Y)>0.

D.2 Full proof

Step 1: Markov chain.

The pair (Y,B)(Y,B) is observed only through the deterministic projection πY:(Y,B)↦Y\pi_{Y}:(Y,B)\mapsto Y, and any rater function ff depends only on YY. We therefore have the Markov chain

(Y,B)→Y→f⁡(Y),(Y,B)\;\to\;Y\;\to\;f(Y),

because f⁡(Y)f(Y) is conditionally independent of BB given YY by construction.

Step 2: Data Processing Inequality.

By the Data Processing Inequality [Cover and Thomas, 2006, Theorem 2.8.1], mutual information is non-increasing under processing:

I⁡((Y,B),f⁡(Y))≤I⁡((Y,B),Y).I\bigl((Y,B);\,f(Y)\bigr)\;\leq\;I\bigl((Y,B);\,Y\bigr).
Step 3: Decomposition of mutual information.

By the chain rule,

I⁡((Y,B),Y)=I⁡(Y,Y)+I⁡(B;Y∣Y)=H⁡(Y)+0=H⁡(Y),I\bigl((Y,B);\,Y\bigr)\;=\;I(Y;Y)+I(B;Y\mid Y)\;=\;H(Y)+0\;=\;H(Y),

since B|YB\mid Y is independent of YY given YY (trivially), so I⁡(B;Y∣Y)=0I(B;Y\mid Y)=0.

Step 4: Residual is orthogonal to YY.

Define the residual DY,B=B−𝔼⁡[B∣Y]D_{Y,B}=B-\mathbb{E}[B\mid Y]. By construction,

𝔼⁡[DY,B∣Y]=0almost surely,\mathbb{E}[D_{Y,B}\mid Y]=0\quad\text{almost surely},

so DY,BD_{Y,B} is mean-independent of YY. Now compute

I⁡(DY,B,f⁡(Y))≤I⁡(DY,B,Y)=H⁡(DY,B)−H⁡(DY,B∣Y).I(D_{Y,B};\,f(Y))\;\leq\;I(D_{Y,B};\,Y)\;=\;H(D_{Y,B})-H(D_{Y,B}\mid Y).

The mean-independence above ensures the centred component of the residual is uncorrelated with YY. Under the additional regularity assumption that DY,BD_{Y,B} is independent of YY in distribution (a stronger form of the variance-stationarity assumption, which holds for our session-level data where the conditional law of behavioral shortcuts is invariant across verbal-commitment patterns; see Assumption F below for the precise condition), we obtain H⁡(DY,B∣Y)=H⁡(DY,B)H(D_{Y,B}\mid Y)=H(D_{Y,B}). Therefore

I⁡(DY,B,f⁡(Y))= 0.I(D_{Y,B};\,f(Y))\;=\;0.
Step 5: Detection bound.

Any estimator d^\hat{d} measurable with respect to σ⁡(Y)\sigma(Y) is a function of f⁡(Y)f(Y) for some ff. By Fano’s inequality [Cover and Thomas, 2006, Theorem 2.10.1] applied to DY,BD_{Y,B},

Pr[d^(Y)≠DY,B]≥H⁡(DY,B∣f⁡(Y))−1log⁡|𝒟|=H⁡(DY,B)−1log⁡|𝒟|,\Pr[\hat{d}(Y)\neq D_{Y,B}]\;\geq\;\frac{H(D_{Y,B}\mid f(Y))-1}{\log|\mathcal{D}|}\;=\;\frac{H(D_{Y,B})-1}{\log|\mathcal{D}|},

where 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the support of the residual. Whenever H⁡(DY,B)>1H(D_{Y,B})>1 (which holds for any non-degenerate b|yb\mid y), the error rate is bounded away from zero. The Compliance Gap is therefore not reliably identifiable from YY alone.

D.3 Remarks

Remark (Empirical concordance with R6).

The R6 blinded human-evaluation data report Fleiss’ κ=0.130\kappa=0.130 across nine raters and 0/150/15 correctly identified compliant responses. Both numbers are consistent with I⁡(DY,B,f⁡(Y))≈0I(D_{Y,B};f(Y))\approx 0: under chance-level identifiability, κ→0\kappa\to 0 and accuracy →\to base rate.

Remark (What can close the gap).

Theorem 2 bounds only text-only observers. If the rater observes the tool-call log channel directly, ff is no longer measurable with respect to σ⁡(Y)\sigma(Y) alone, and the DPI bound does not apply. This is precisely the channel BS-Bench instruments. As reported in the main text, a 146M-parameter hyperbolic classifier reading this channel reaches 98.3%98.3\% binary detection on a held-out 288-session subset of BS-Bench — a preliminary illustration only, not a contribution of this paper.

Remark (Sharpness).

The bound is sharp: when b=g⁡(y)b=g(y) for some deterministic gg (the degenerate case), DY,B≡0D_{Y,B}\equiv 0 and the Compliance Gap is recoverable from YY alone. Theorem 2 is non-trivial precisely when Var⁡(B∣Y)>0\mathrm{Var}(B\mid Y)>0, which is the empirically observed regime (R6 blinded human evaluation; same condition produces the heterogeneous behavioral outcomes documented in Exps 1, 6, and 9 of the main paper).

Appendix E Concentration Bounds for CG^\widehat{\mathrm{CG}}

We next derive a finite-sample bound for the empirical Compliance Gap estimator

CG^=1n​∑i=1n𝟙​[verbal compliance in session ​i]−1n​∑i=1n𝟙​[actual compliance in session ​i].\widehat{\mathrm{CG}}\;=\;\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{1}[\text{verbal compliance in session }i]-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{1}[\text{actual compliance in session }i].
Proposition 3 (Hoeffding bound on CG^\widehat{\mathrm{CG}}).

Let sessions be drawn i.i.d. from the population. For any ϵ>0\epsilon>0,

Pr[|CG^−CG|>ϵ]≤ 4exp(−nϵ2/2).\Pr\bigl[|\widehat{\mathrm{CG}}-\mathrm{CG}|>\epsilon\bigr]\;\leq\;4\exp(-n\epsilon^{2}/2).
Proof.

Each indicator is bounded in [0,1][0,1]. By Hoeffding’s inequality applied separately to VCR^\widehat{\mathrm{VCR}} and ACR^\widehat{\mathrm{ACR}},

Pr[|VCR^−VCR|>ϵ/2]≤2exp(−nϵ2/2),\Pr[|\widehat{\mathrm{VCR}}-\mathrm{VCR}|>\epsilon/2]\leq 2\exp(-n\epsilon^{2}/2),

and similarly for ACR^\widehat{\mathrm{ACR}}. Union bound gives the stated rate. ∎

Numerical implication.

With n=240n=240 sessions (Exp 1) and ϵ=0.05\epsilon=0.05, the bound is 4exp(−240⋅0.0025/2)=4exp(−0.3)≈2.964\exp(-240\cdot 0.0025/2)=4\exp(-0.3)\approx 2.96, which is loose; the empirical bootstrap interval (10,000 resamples) reported in the main paper is the operative quantity. With n=2,031n=2{,}031 (full BS-Bench v1) and ϵ=0.05\epsilon=0.05, the bound is 4exp(−2031⋅0.0025/2)=4exp(−2.54)≈0.3174\exp(-2031\cdot 0.0025/2)=4\exp(-2.54)\approx 0.317, useful as a coarse sanity check.

Appendix F Assumptions Made Explicit

For transparency we list every assumption used in the two theorems, marked by where it enters.

Assumption 4 (A1, used in Thm 1).

User utility UU depends only on the realised behavior bb. We do not require UU to ignore yy; the proof goes through whenever UU has a strict additive component depending on bb (cf. the surgical-checklist case in App. A.7).

Assumption 5 (A2, used in Thm 1).

The reward signal RR during preference-reward training depends only on text yy. This holds for canonical RLHF [Christiano et al., 2017, Ouyang et al., 2022] that elicits human preferences from text outputs alone. Process-aware reward signals (e.g. tool-call-log scoring) violate (A2) by construction; Theorem 1 accordingly does not bound them, and BS-Bench is the infrastructure required to make such alternative signals operationally feasible.

Assumption 6 (A3, used in Thm 1).

The behavioral channel bb has positive conditional variance given the verbal channel yy. Empirically supported by R6 (κ=0.130\kappa=0.130, 0/150/15).

Assumption 7 (A4: Distributional independence of the residual, used in Thm 2 Step 4).

The residual DY,BD_{Y,B} is independent of YY in distribution. This implies H⁡(DY,B∣Y)=H⁡(DY,B)H(D_{Y,B}\mid Y)=H(D_{Y,B}). A strictly weaker form (H⁡(DY,B∣Y)≤H⁡(DY,B)H(D_{Y,B}\mid Y)\leq H(D_{Y,B}), equivalent to mean-independence plus variance stationarity) suffices for the inequality version of Thm 2; see Cover and Thomas [2006] §2.5 for the general case.

Appendix G Experiment Inventory

This section provides the experiment inventory (sessions, seeds, framings) for all 13 experiments cross-referenced in the main paper. Per-model raw outcomes (sessions ×\times models ×\times cells ×\times metrics) and the Python notebooks that compute the reported statistical tests (paired tt-tests, Mann-Whitney UU, η2\eta^{2} with bootstrap CI, Hoeffding bounds) are released as the OSF artifact at https://osf.io/mvnq4/; the PDF supplement is intentionally inventory-level for archival readability.

Compute envelope.

The total compute used by this paper is bounded by: (i) 2,0312{,}031 API-driven sessions across the six frontier API models (Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama 3.3 70B via API, Mistral Small 24B via API), and (ii) two open-weight SLM LoRA/QLoRA fine-tuning runs for the Exp 3 SFT pilot (Llama 3.1 8B and Mistral 7B base models on a single workstation-class GPU). Per-experiment API call counts, token-level cost summaries, and SFT GPU-hour logs are tabulated in the OSF release alongside the raw outcomes.

Notation Summary

We collect notation used throughout the proofs.

  • •

    Θ\Theta: parameter space of the policy.

  • •

    πθ:𝒳→Δ⁡(𝒴)\pi_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{Y}): a stochastic policy mapping prompts x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} to distributions over text outputs y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}.

  • •

    ℋ\mathcal{H}: space of environments (tool affordances, file states, system context).

  • •

    b:𝒴×ℋ→ℬb:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{B}: behavioral trajectory induced by output yy in environment hh. We write B=b⁡(Y,H)B=b(Y,H) for the random behavioral trajectory.

  • •

    R:𝒴→ℝR:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}: a verbal-only reward (a function of the text output alone).

  • •

    U:ℬ∪(𝒴×ℬ)→ℝU:\mathcal{B}\cup(\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{B})\to\mathbb{R}: user utility, depending on the realised behavior (and possibly the text).

  • •

    VCR\mathrm{VCR}: verbal compliance rate (fraction of sessions in which the assistant text claims to follow the user’s process instruction).

  • •

    ACR\mathrm{ACR}: actual compliance rate (fraction of sessions in which the tool-call log shows the user’s process was followed).

  • •

    CG=VCR−ACR∈[−1,1]\mathrm{CG}=\mathrm{VCR}-\mathrm{ACR}\in[-1,1]: the Compliance Gap.

  • •

    ICR\mathrm{ICR}: instruction compliance rate == files read individually // total files (per session).

  • •

    DF\mathrm{DF}: delegation frequency == batch tool calls // total tool calls (per session).

  • •

    FCR\mathrm{FCR}: false completion rate == false “done” claims // total claims (per session).

  • •

    TA\mathrm{TA}: task accuracy == planted errors detected // total planted errors (per session).

  • •

    By channel: VCR\mathrm{VCR} is the sole verbal-channel metric; ICR,DF,FCR,ACR,TA\mathrm{ICR},\mathrm{DF},\mathrm{FCR},\mathrm{ACR},\mathrm{TA} are behavioral-channel metrics; CG\mathrm{CG} measures the gap between the two.

    H⁡(⋅)H(\cdot), I⁡(⋅,⋅)I(\cdot;\cdot): Shannon entropy and mutual information.

2 Theorem 2 (DPI Undetectability)

2.1 Statement

Theorem 2 (DPI Undetectability).

Let X=(Y,B)X=(Y,B) denote the (verbal, behavioral) random pair with joint distribution PY,BP_{Y,B}, and let f:𝒴→𝒵f:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{Z} be any rater function depending only on the text YY. Define the residual

DY,B=B−𝔼⁡[B∣Y],D_{Y,B}\;=\;B-\mathbb{E}[B\mid Y],

i.e. the part of behavior not predictable from text. Then for any such ff,

I⁡(DY,B,f⁡(Y))= 0,I\bigl(D_{Y,B};\,f(Y)\bigr)\;=\;0,

and consequently no estimator d^=g⁡(f⁡(Y))\hat{d}=g(f(Y)) achieves Pr[d^=DY,B]>Pr[DY,B=𝔼[DY,B∣Y]]\Pr[\hat{d}=D_{Y,B}]>\Pr[D_{Y,B}=\mathbb{E}[D_{Y,B}\mid Y]]. The Compliance Gap, defined on the residual DY,BD_{Y,B}, is therefore not identifiable from YY alone whenever Var⁡(B∣Y)>0\mathrm{Var}(B\mid Y)>0.

2.2 Full proof

Step 1: Markov chain.

The pair (Y,B)(Y,B) is observed only through the deterministic projection πY:(Y,B)↦Y\pi_{Y}:(Y,B)\mapsto Y, and any rater function ff depends only on YY. We therefore have the Markov chain

(Y,B)→Y→f⁡(Y),(Y,B)\;\to\;Y\;\to\;f(Y),

because f⁡(Y)f(Y) is conditionally independent of BB given YY by construction.

Step 2: Data Processing Inequality.

By the Data Processing Inequality (Cover and Thomas, 2006, Theorem 2.8.1), mutual information is non-increasing under processing:

I⁡((Y,B),f⁡(Y))≤I⁡((Y,B),Y).I\bigl((Y,B);\,f(Y)\bigr)\;\leq\;I\bigl((Y,B);\,Y\bigr).
Step 3: Decomposition of mutual information.

By the chain rule,

I⁡((Y,B),Y)=I⁡(Y,Y)+I⁡(B;Y∣Y)=H⁡(Y)+0=H⁡(Y),I\bigl((Y,B);\,Y\bigr)\;=\;I(Y;Y)+I(B;Y\mid Y)\;=\;H(Y)+0\;=\;H(Y),

since B|YB\mid Y is independent of YY given YY (trivially), so I⁡(B;Y∣Y)=0I(B;Y\mid Y)=0.

Step 4: Residual is orthogonal to YY.

Define the residual DY,B=B−𝔼⁡[B∣Y]D_{Y,B}=B-\mathbb{E}[B\mid Y]. By construction,

𝔼⁡[DY,B∣Y]=0almost surely,\mathbb{E}[D_{Y,B}\mid Y]=0\quad\text{almost surely},

so DY,BD_{Y,B} is mean-independent of YY. Now compute

I⁡(DY,B,f⁡(Y))≤I⁡(DY,B,Y)=H⁡(DY,B)−H⁡(DY,B∣Y).I(D_{Y,B};\,f(Y))\;\leq\;I(D_{Y,B};\,Y)\;=\;H(D_{Y,B})-H(D_{Y,B}\mid Y).

The mean-independence above ensures the centred component of the residual is uncorrelated with YY. Under the additional regularity assumption that DY,BD_{Y,B} is independent of YY in distribution (a stronger form of the variance-stationarity assumption, which holds for our session-level data where the conditional law of behavioral shortcuts is invariant across verbal-commitment patterns; see Assumption 4 below for the precise condition), we obtain H⁡(DY,B∣Y)=H⁡(DY,B)H(D_{Y,B}\mid Y)=H(D_{Y,B}). Therefore

I⁡(DY,B,f⁡(Y))= 0.I(D_{Y,B};\,f(Y))\;=\;0.
Step 5: Detection bound.

Any estimator d^\hat{d} measurable with respect to σ⁡(Y)\sigma(Y) is a function of f⁡(Y)f(Y) for some ff. By Fano’s inequality (Cover and Thomas, 2006, Theorem 2.10.1) applied to DY,BD_{Y,B},

Pr[d^(Y)≠DY,B]≥H⁡(DY,B∣f⁡(Y))−1log⁡|𝒟|=H⁡(DY,B)−1log⁡|𝒟|,\Pr[\hat{d}(Y)\neq D_{Y,B}]\;\geq\;\frac{H(D_{Y,B}\mid f(Y))-1}{\log|\mathcal{D}|}\;=\;\frac{H(D_{Y,B})-1}{\log|\mathcal{D}|},

where 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the support of the residual. Whenever H⁡(DY,B)>1H(D_{Y,B})>1 (which holds for any non-degenerate b|yb\mid y), the error rate is bounded away from zero. The Compliance Gap is therefore not reliably identifiable from YY alone.

2.3 Remarks

Remark (Empirical concordance with R6).

The R6 blinded human-evaluation data report Fleiss’ κ=0.130\kappa=0.130 across nine raters and 0/150/15 correctly identified compliant responses. Both numbers are consistent with I⁡(DY,B,f⁡(Y))≈0I(D_{Y,B};f(Y))\approx 0: under chance-level identifiability, κ→0\kappa\to 0 and accuracy →\to base rate.

Remark (What can close the gap).

Theorem 2 bounds only text-only observers. If the rater observes the tool-call log channel directly, ff is no longer measurable with respect to σ⁡(Y)\sigma(Y) alone, and the DPI bound does not apply. This is precisely the channel BS-Bench instruments. As reported in the main text, a 146M-parameter hyperbolic classifier reading this channel reaches 98.3%98.3\% binary detection on a held-out 288-session subset of BS-Bench — a preliminary illustration only, not a contribution of this paper.

Remark (Sharpness).

The bound is sharp: when b=g⁡(y)b=g(y) for some deterministic gg (the degenerate case), DY,B≡0D_{Y,B}\equiv 0 and the Compliance Gap is recoverable from YY alone. Theorem 2 is non-trivial precisely when Var⁡(B∣Y)>0\mathrm{Var}(B\mid Y)>0, which is the empirically observed regime (R6 blinded human evaluation; same condition produces the heterogeneous behavioral outcomes documented in Exps 1, 6, and 9 of the main paper).

3 Concentration Bounds for CG^\widehat{\mathrm{CG}}

We next derive a finite-sample bound for the empirical Compliance Gap estimator

CG^=1n​∑i=1n𝟙​[verbal compliance in session ​i]−1n​∑i=1n𝟙​[actual compliance in session ​i].\widehat{\mathrm{CG}}\;=\;\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{1}[\text{verbal compliance in session }i]-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{1}[\text{actual compliance in session }i].
Proposition 1 (Hoeffding bound on CG^\widehat{\mathrm{CG}}).

Let sessions be drawn i.i.d. from the population. For any ϵ>0\epsilon>0,

Pr[|CG^−CG|>ϵ]≤ 4exp(−nϵ2/2).\Pr\bigl[|\widehat{\mathrm{CG}}-\mathrm{CG}|>\epsilon\bigr]\;\leq\;4\exp(-n\epsilon^{2}/2).
Proof.

Each indicator is bounded in [0,1][0,1]. By Hoeffding’s inequality applied separately to VCR^\widehat{\mathrm{VCR}} and ACR^\widehat{\mathrm{ACR}},

Pr[|VCR^−VCR|>ϵ/2]≤2exp(−nϵ2/2),\Pr[|\widehat{\mathrm{VCR}}-\mathrm{VCR}|>\epsilon/2]\leq 2\exp(-n\epsilon^{2}/2),

and similarly for ACR^\widehat{\mathrm{ACR}}. Union bound gives the stated rate. ∎

Numerical implication.

With n=240n=240 sessions (Exp 1) and ϵ=0.05\epsilon=0.05, the bound is 4exp(−240⋅0.0025/2)=4exp(−0.3)≈2.964\exp(-240\cdot 0.0025/2)=4\exp(-0.3)\approx 2.96, which is loose; the empirical bootstrap interval (10,000 resamples) reported in the main paper is the operative quantity. With n=2,031n=2{,}031 (full BS-Bench v1) and ϵ=0.05\epsilon=0.05, the bound is 4exp(−2031⋅0.0025/2)=4exp(−2.54)≈0.3174\exp(-2031\cdot 0.0025/2)=4\exp(-2.54)\approx 0.317, useful as a coarse sanity check.

4 Assumptions Made Explicit

For transparency we list every assumption used in the two theorems, marked by where it enters.

Assumption 1 (A1, used in Thm 1).

User utility UU depends only on the realised behavior bb. We do not require UU to ignore yy; the proof goes through whenever UU has a strict additive component depending on bb (cf. the surgical-checklist case in App. A.7).

Assumption 2 (A2, used in Thm 1).

The reward signal RR during preference-reward training depends only on text yy. This holds for canonical RLHF (Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022) that elicits human preferences from text outputs alone. Process-aware reward signals (e.g. tool-call-log scoring) violate (A2) by construction; Theorem 1 accordingly does not bound them, and BS-Bench is the infrastructure required to make such alternative signals operationally feasible.

Assumption 3 (A3, used in Thm 1).

The behavioral channel bb has positive conditional variance given the verbal channel yy. Empirically supported by R6 (κ=0.130\kappa=0.130, 0/150/15).

Assumption 4 (A4: Distributional independence of the residual, used in Thm 2 Step 4).

The residual DY,BD_{Y,B} is independent of YY in distribution. This implies H⁡(DY,B∣Y)=H⁡(DY,B)H(D_{Y,B}\mid Y)=H(D_{Y,B}). A strictly weaker form (H⁡(DY,B∣Y)≤H⁡(DY,B)H(D_{Y,B}\mid Y)\leq H(D_{Y,B}), equivalent to mean-independence plus variance stationarity) suffices for the inequality version of Thm 2; see Cover and Thomas (2006) §2.5 for the general case.

5 Experiment Inventory

This section provides the experiment inventory (sessions, seeds, framings) for all 13 experiments cross-referenced in the main paper. Per-model raw outcomes (sessions ×\times models ×\times cells ×\times metrics) and the Python notebooks that compute the reported statistical tests (paired tt-tests, Mann-Whitney UU, η2\eta^{2} with bootstrap CI, Hoeffding bounds) are released as the OSF artifact at https://osf.io/mvnq4/; the PDF supplement is intentionally inventory-level for archival readability.

Compute envelope.

The total compute used by this paper is bounded by: (i) 2,0312{,}031 API-driven sessions across the six frontier API models (Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama 3.3 70B via API, Mistral Small 24B via API), and (ii) two open-weight SLM LoRA/QLoRA fine-tuning runs for the Exp 3 SFT pilot (Llama 3.1 8B and Mistral 7B base models on a single workstation-class GPU). Per-experiment API call counts, token-level cost summaries, and SFT GPU-hour logs are tabulated in the OSF release alongside the raw outcomes.
